"Knowing the identity behind a crawler tells us relatively little about whether its behavior is harmful. Under the New York bill, a company that discloses its identity and then accesses the website 10,000 times a minute complies with the law even though it is still imposing enormous and likely unjustified costs on the site. But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not."

It does seem like this bill mostly affects normal users and is suspect with more surveillance being pushed. However the biggest problem is that the internet is global and the fees only apply to the US. If bots from Russia, China, India, or even France are scrapping then how would this even reduce the bots? Seems more like a new 'contempt of business model' is the purpose of this bill.

This is exactly what companies like DataDome do, and sometimes Cloudflare continues to, when their bot protection pages enter endless loops. They don't even realize they are ruining the UX for thousands of legitimate users with their faulty JS browser fingerprinting verifications.

Genuinely asking here: is there a future where we end up with a version of the open web where everything isn’t paywalled or ID gated?

The article mentions the IETF is working on standards to deal with the proposed legislature and frustration of site operators. Almost any solution is going to be at the expense of user convenience and privacy. I see two interesting solutions mentioned here: micropayments, and proof-of-work. It seems unlikely the future of the open web will land on either. Both are inconvenient but at least could be done by anybody, potentially in a privacy preserving way. Using reputation based decentralized identity is another one (eg. proving you’re coming from a web domain or group), that seems more inconvenient for the platform because of false positives that could come through.

Meanwhile, a worse outcome is requiring attested hardware to get access to anything on the web. This already exists from the media companies pushing for controlled access to streaming. Netflix requires an hardware attested device to stream in 4K. Imagine a future where you now need one to read a New York Times article.

I can see some pushback against the alternatives (eg. digital ID), but if privacy preserving proofs are built in from the get go, it’s much better than not being able to see recipes because I have a rooted Android.

If you have an endpoint with interesting information and you don't want it spammed with requests, require a proof of work from the client, scale up the hardness of it as the load goes up so it never exceeds what's comfortable for you. Even a hard proof of work won't slow down somebody that makes one request per second because they are reading the site but will sighificantly interfere with crawlers that hit you 10000 a second currently at very little cost to them.

The module doing proof of work might be a part of your frontend that is static and on CDN.

If you want agents still have access to your data, just not through scraping, provide alternative format for them. Like periodic sqlite dump.

I made a prototype of such PoW two years ago. A challenge is a random number. Checking the client's solution is calculating one hash of the challenge glued to client's solution and checking if the resulting hash is less than a specific value. The lower the value, the harder the task for the client to do. Client needs to calculate this hash multiple times to find a response that will result (when glued with challenge) with low enough hash.

The server needs to keep short lived cache with challenges so the client can't just make up one or reuse another solution and provide two responses for every challenge, first, very small and fast with a challenge, and the second one with actual content (if response was correct). Nothing much worse than CORS preflight.

Scale seems to be the real issue.  Given that there are relatively few actors with the scale to cause serious problems (and those actors have the resources to shrug off minor penalties), perhaps more targeted legislation is necessary.  e.g. Different penalties for petty scraping and grand theft scraping.  Of course, this would necessarily target the people who pay for election campaigns, so it will never happen.

This would be a stronger argument if it hadn't been made for decades by the industry exploiting the open web with bad bots. Every pro-freedom article rings hollow when we've seen the tech world act nothing but extractively and without restraint.
